subtopics.title: Convection in fluids: buoyancy, circulation and model selection
subtopics.learning_goal: Natural convection arises when buoyancy acts on density variations and geometry permits fluid motion; stable layering and forced flow alter the transport model.

qrt_targets.protected_work: Explain contrasting circulation through actual density, buoyancy and mass continuity, including an exception where temperature alone gives the wrong direction.
qrt_targets.decisive_route: Tank A has warm lower fluid density 990 and cool upper fluid density 1000 kg/m³. Tank B has a warm salty lower layer density 1010 and a cool upper layer density 1000. Predict which arrangement develops buoyancy-driven mixing, describe return flow, and explain why equal heating labels are insufficient. Shortest valid route: A is unstable: lighter lower fluid rises and denser upper fluid descends. B has denser lower fluid and is stable against small vertical exchange; warmth does not override composition-dependent density. In a closed tank upward mass flux has compensating downward flux.

core1a.phenomenon: A fluid heated from below can circulate, while comparable heating from above may produce stable layering.
core1a.scientific_narrative:
Conduction transfers energy through microscopic interactions without a bulk flow of matter. Convection transfers energy by the motion of fluid parcels. A fluid parcel that is warmer than neighbouring fluid often expands at approximately the local pressure, making its density smaller. In a gravitational field the surrounding fluid exerts a buoyant force equal to the weight of displaced fluid. When that force exceeds the parcel's weight, an upward tendency results. A cooler denser parcel may tend downward. This is a model of natural convection; it depends on the equation of state, gravity and surrounding density, not on a universal slogan that every hot object rises.

Imagine two layers of the same ordinary fluid. If the lower layer is warmed and becomes less dense than the upper layer, a small upward displacement can allow it to continue rising; denser fluid replaces it below. A return flow is needed because matter is conserved in a closed container. If the lighter layer already lies above the denser layer, small vertical displacements instead tend to be opposed by buoyancy. This stable arrangement can reduce natural convection even when the layers have different temperatures. Heat can still transfer by conduction or radiation.

A fan or pump can drive flow even without the density contrast that sustains natural convection. This is forced convection. When moving air passes a warm surface, energy can be transferred between the surface and air, then carried away. Faster flow often increases heat loss under comparable conditions, but an observation of faster cooling alone cannot identify the exact mechanism: evaporation, area, radiation or initial temperatures might differ. The existing Core2 fuse candidate assumes lateral heat loss and neglects end conduction. Treat that as a conditional model; this unit teaches the convection prerequisite and a separate experimental reasoning construction.

For a small parcel of volume V surrounded by fluid of density ρ_s, the simplified net vertical force relative to weight is (ρ_s−ρ_p)gV upward, before drag or other constraints. Do not turn this into a terminal-speed prediction without resistance and geometry. In water close to 4 °C the ordinary monotonic density-temperature relation can fail, and mixtures can have salinity or composition gradients. Establish which layer is actually denser. A credible explanation identifies the energy path, the density contrast, the buoyancy direction, the return path and the limits of the model.

derivation_steps.action: Compare actual density of a parcel with its surroundings at the same level.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Buoyant force follows displaced fluid weight, not temperature alone.

derivation_steps.action: Determine direction of net buoyancy and stability of layer arrangement.
derivation_steps.why_valid: A displaced parcel rises if lighter than its surroundings and sinks if heavier.

derivation_steps.action: Close the flow path and trace energy transported with matter.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Mass is conserved in a closed vessel; rising flow requires compensating return flow.

derivation_steps.action: Distinguish natural and forced convection and test alternative heat-loss paths.
derivation_steps.why_valid: A pump adds mechanical forcing; conduction and radiation can persist without circulation.

Parcel buoyancy assumes local hydrostatic surroundings and a small parcel; drag, boundaries and pressure fields affect flow.
Natural convection needs gravity, a destabilizing density arrangement and freedom to move; forced convection need not.
Heat loss may combine multiple paths; rate comparisons require controlled area, temperature and environment.

progressive_examples.problem: A parcel of volume 0.002 m³ has density 980 kg/m³; its surroundings have density 1000 kg/m³. Use g=10 m/s². Find net buoyancy.
progressive_examples.independent_check: Parcel weight 19.6 N; buoyant force 20 N.

progressive_examples.problem: A vessel contains a lighter upper layer and denser lower layer. An identical vessel has the lighter layer below. Which is more susceptible to natural mixing?
progressive_examples.reasoning: The second: lighter fluid tends to rise and heavier fluid descends. First is stable against small vertical displacements.
progressive_examples.independent_check: Swap a parcel mentally across the interface and check its restoring or destabilizing buoyancy.

progressive_examples.problem: Two equal dry warm plates cool in still air and fan-driven air. Initial temperatures, areas and surroundings match. Fan-driven plate needs 30 W more input to remain at the same temperature. What follows?
progressive_examples.reasoning: Net extra loss is 30 W under steady balance. Forced convection is a plausible cause, but separate radiation and any changing conductive path before assigning the whole difference.
progressive_examples.independent_check: An independent fan-off repeat or heat-flux measurement can test reproducibility.

figures.scene_description: Light layer above heavy layer is stable; the inverted arrangement permits rising light parcels and descending heavy parcels. Original inline SVG, not source examination figure.

misconception.wrong_model: Warm fluid always rises regardless of surrounding density; every faster cooling observation proves convection.
misconception.diagnostic: A warm parcel is denser than its surroundings because of dissolved material. Which way does buoyancy act?
misconception.repair: Use measured densities and separate mechanisms through controls.

exit_check.task: A parcel is 1.5 kg/m³ less dense than neighbouring air and has volume 0.04 m³, g=10 m/s². What is its simplified net buoyancy?
exit_check.reasoning: Density difference × volume × g; no prediction of terminal speed without drag.

core1b.fresh_task: Two vertical vessels have identical bottom heating. In one the lower liquid density becomes 960 and upper density 980; in the other dissolved solute keeps lower density 1000 and upper 980 kg/m³. Explain different circulation tendencies and specify the physical observation needed to check the model.
core1b.protected_work: Explain contrasting circulation through actual density, buoyancy and mass continuity, including an exception where temperature alone gives the wrong direction.

stages.predict: Predict whether the two bottom-heated vessels circulate similarly or differently. Record an initial reason before explaining the flow.
stages.attempt: Two vertical vessels have identical bottom heating. In one the lower liquid density becomes 960 and upper density 980; in the other dissolved solute keeps lower density 1000 and upper 980 kg/m³. Explain different circulation tendencies and specify the physical observation needed to check the model.
stages.reconstruct: First lower layer is lighter and unstable; second heavier below is stable against small displacements. Observe density at matched depth or trace parcels and return flow. Heating direction alone is not sufficient.
stages.diagnose: If you inferred flow from temperature alone, compare the actual lower and upper densities. Which displacement is self-reinforcing, and where must displaced fluid return?
stages.repair: Reconstruct the density comparison, buoyancy direction and mass-continuity path. Then check whether an externally driven flow changes the conclusion about natural stability.
stages.boundary_test: If the density gradient reverses after prolonged heating, how would the expected circulation change?

core1b.fresh_task: A dry heated surface stays at a fixed temperature with 12 W in an enclosure. A fan raises needed input to 20 W; rotating the surface with fan off raises it to 15 W. Tracer motion appears only during the latter two observations. Evaluate the explanations and design a control.
core1b.protected_work: Choose a natural, forced or nonconvective heat-transfer explanation from controlled temperature and flow observations rather than merely fit cooling rate.

stages.predict: Would you attribute the changes in the three power readings to one process or several? Record an initial interpretation.
stages.attempt: A dry heated surface stays at a fixed temperature with 12 W in an enclosure. A fan raises needed input to 20 W; rotating the surface with fan off raises it to 15 W. Tracer motion appears only during the latter two observations. Evaluate the explanations and design a control.
stages.reconstruct: Steady losses 12,20,15 W. Fan adds 8 W and rotation adds 3 W relative to baseline, with flow evidence supporting forced/natural convection respectively. Radiation or support conduction may still change; match surface surroundings, supports and emissivity.
stages.diagnose: Check whether your model uses steady net input as a measure of total loss, or incorrectly identifies all loss as convection. Which observation distinguishes flow from the other paths?
stages.repair: Compare energy rates at matched temperatures and trace the observed fluid motion. Treat uncontrolled radiation, evaporation or conduction as alternative explanations until controlled.
stages.boundary_test: What if the surface is wet and evaporation changes when the fan runs?

core1b.fresh_task: Two warm water tanks cool at different rates. One is stirred, one is not. The stirred tank has a larger exposed surface and starts hotter. A report says forced convection alone explains the difference. Assess identifiability and propose a fair experiment.
core1b.protected_work: Judge whether a measured temperature or cooling difference identifies a convection mechanism, using counterexamples and a discriminating control.

stages.predict: Would the reported stirred-tank comparison convince you that stirring alone caused the cooling difference? Record your initial judgement.
stages.attempt: Two warm water tanks cool at different rates. One is stirred, one is not. The stirred tank has a larger exposed surface and starts hotter. A report says forced convection alone explains the difference. Assess identifiability and propose a fair experiment.
stages.reconstruct: Multiple confounds (temperature difference, exposed area, evaporation, stirring). Match mass, area, initial temperature, surroundings and cover; vary stirring only, measure temperature/time and mass loss or steady input. Stirring can alter internal transfer but alone not established.
stages.diagnose: Locate any causal claim that uses the observed cooling rate alone. Can a separate process produce the same observation while circulation persists?
stages.repair: Build a counterexample, then propose a matched comparison changing only the target fluid motion and recording mass loss or input power as appropriate.
stages.boundary_test: If the controlled trials agree in cooling rate, does that prove no internal convection exists?
